newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian oil refinery margins shrink further.
newsitem.headline: Australian oil refinery margins shrink further.

text.p: Australia's petroleum refiners saw their profit margins shrink to half an Australian cent per litre of product in calendar 1996 from 0.8 cents in 1995, according to an independent report issued on Thursday.
Costs have also fallen, down to 5.5 cents per litre in 1996, but these were not enough to keep pace with the intense price competition being felt in the market for petrol, it said.
These costs were calculated using operating, production and marketing expenses. They excluded the volatile cost of crude oil, the report said.
Australia's eight refineries have total daily capacity of around 800,000 barrels. About 70 to 80 percent of the refineries' production is made up of land transport fuels.
The report, prepared for the Australian Institute of Petroleum by accountants Ernst and Young, concluded that the level of refinery profitability was unsustainable.
The main price competition has come in the market for petrol (gasoline), where aggressive independents are challenging the four Australian-based refiners' control over retail distribution.
Australia's eight refineries are run by the Royal Dutch/Shell Group, Mobil Corp, The British Petroleum Co Plc and Ampol, a joint venture between Caltex Australia Ltd and Pioneer International Ltd.
They face stiff competition from independent distributors which are selling a lot of imported product, taking advantage of cheaply priced Asian petrol.

"If petrol is being sold at a bargain-basement price out of Singapore, and costs of the Australian refiners are higher than Singapore, then their margins are being squeezed to virtually nothing," institute executive director Jim Starkey told Reuters.
The institute is using the report to call on the government to give the refiners a freer hand to reshape their distribution networks and be allowed to operate more of their own outlets.
Canberra is currently considering proposals to deregulate the industry.
